newsitem.title: USA: Commonwealth set for stormy Nigeria meeting.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth set for stormy Nigeria meeting.

text.p: Commonwealth ministers were to open a two-day meeting on Saturday on how best to push Nigeria back into the democratic fold, but tempers looked set to fray as sharp differences between the participants emerged.
The eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) was due to start talks at 7:30 p.m. (2330 GMT) in New York and continue discussions for much of Sunday.

Analysts expected results to depend largely on Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, whose frustration with what he saw as foot-dragging by other members boiled over a few days ago when he denounced "appeasers" in the 53-nation grouping.
"We'll have our discussion this weekend, but it seems to me they're simply setting the scenario for another delay," he told the Toronto Globe and Mail newspaper.
"Time is getting awfully short."

The Commonwealth, a grouping of Britain and its former colonies and protectorates, suspended oil-rich Nigeria last November after the execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority-rights activists.

But since then differences have appeared and relations among CMAG states were further eroded last month when they called off a fact-finding mission after Nigeria refused to let ministers meet human rights campaigners and opposition groups.

Canada and others felt there was little hope of engaging Nigeria in meaningful dialogue and wanted to impose a set of sanctions that were agreed to in April but frozen in order to give the military government more time to talk.
But others were opposed to excluding the populous west African nation from the fold, saying limited dialogue was better than nothing at all.
Axworthy said CMAG had a number of proposals to discuss before it could make recommendations about further talks with the military government of General Sani Abacha.
"If this could be productive, that's good, and if not, let's go ahead with the measures (the agreed sanctions)," he told reporters late on Friday.
"If the role of a CMAG mission (to Nigeria) were restricted to meeting officials, then we've been there before and it wouldn't serve our purpose of getting a broader image of Nigeria," he said.
But Nigeria -- which insisted on discussing its suspension from the Commonwealth before any other topic -- seemed unlikely to change its mind about any future CMAG mission.
"I don't think the Nigerians are prepared to let the delegation meet anyone other than officials," said one Commonwealth diplomat.

The London-based Human Rights Watch/Africa group on Friday released a stinging 52-page denunciation of Nigeria's planned three-year transition to democracy and called on CMAG to impose sanctions on Abuja.

Axworthy announced in June that Canada would unilaterally impose the sanctions -- which included a ban on sporting links and arms sales -- but experts said the only measure to have any effect would be an world-wide embargo on oil sales.
Britain and New Zealand, among others, opposed the idea of an oil embargo on the grounds that it would hurt ordinary Nigerians and not their leaders.
"As we've seen before when these kind of measures have been imposed, it's almost impossible to completely seal off a country," said one British official.
And an oil embargo would only work with the support of the United States, which buys 40 percent of its oil from Nigeria.
CMAG comprises Malaysia, Zimbabwe, Jamaica, Ghana, Britain, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada.
